What should i know about moving/living an apartment for the first time?
Pay your rent on time. This may seem obvious but its the most I portant thing.
My contract has a $50 late fee if the rent isn't paid on the day it is due. Very good incentive to pay on time.

MAKE COPIES OF EVERYTHING. Any document that involves a transaction relating to the rental, make a copy, a letter from the landlord/business, make a copy, etc. And then keep them all organized and files so if you have a dispute, you have a physical copy of an agreement or notice. Also, mark your calendar for the date by which you need to renew your lease or declare your intent to not renew.
This. Yes. Hard copies saved my ass a time or two.

Take pictures of the problems with the apartment when you move in. Even if you have to fill out a sheet telling them the problems, always have pictures.

If you cook, do your dishes. I cook, some roommates get a real stick in their ass about it.

1. The upstairs neighbors will make noise that you won't like (solution: live on top floor).
  2. The downstairs neighbors will not like the noise that you make (solution: live on ground floor).
  3. Read the lease in its entirety.
  4. Living with roommates can be a nightmare if they decide to make it one. Choose carefully.
  5. Look up or ask existing residents how promptly and successfully maintenance work is performed.

Maintain a good relationship with the building manager or landlord. Be cordial and respectful whenever you're around him. Others have already said to make copies of important documents in case of any disputes. Being kind may help you avoid those disputes all together, you never know when you'll have a vindictive landlord.

To compound on this, the maintenance folk as well. Be kind and courteous to them, and if they arent complete human waste, they'll see your unit number at take care of it quickly. I regularly spoke to the Maintenance people in passing (about their day etc) and when my a.c. went out, they fixed it within an hour of my request.
Make nice with your neighbors, never know when you'll be in a bind and need someone's help. It's way easier to ask for help or a favor if you've met before.
Don't let someone stay more than one night unless you can live with them long term or they sign their name to the lease. Friends. Girls. Family. Anyone.
Buy a toilet plunger before you need one.
Keep it clean. Doing a bit every day beats having to do a mass cleaning once a month. You'll also be able to have people over when you are not living in a shit hole.

Always test the water pressure and temperature of the shower. I lived in a place with an awful shower for a year and was completely miserable. It sounds so silly, but waking up every morning to a pathetic trickle of water that constantly changed temperature from boiling hot to ice cold nearly drove me insane. It is the first thing I check when moving into a new place. I would also recommend going out and buying a nice fancy shower head. They are cheap, easy to set up, and can be a massive improvement over what the landlord has installed.

I would also recommend going out and buying a nice fancy shower head

This is a great idea, as shower heads can get pretty nasty inside and are usually never cleaned.

Don't forget that when you buy a shower head, you can also remove the water pressure regulator / flow restrictor to make it spray harder. The EPA requires all shower heads to come with a plastic thing to limit the amount of water that can rush through. You can remove it with a pair of pliers. Some are screwed in, others are glued in. There's some short videos on youtube on how to do that, but you can probably figure it out.

Test your smoke alarms and make sure the batteries are good.

Pack up the blinds that came with the place, wrap them up nicely, and put in new ones. Don't break anything. Those blinds coulod be 20+ years old and fragile to the touch, but if you damage them you're looking at $30+ for new ones - go pick some up at the Family Dollar. Worth it.

Don't fuck loudly in rooms directly connected to the neighbor's bedrooms (or the room of their children-dear god, most awkward conversation). It's common courtesy and makes you a good neighbor.

You don't need a big place, you just need a safe place. Don't move into the ghetto in a rush to get out - you'll regret it. Don't get a roommate if you can avoid it.
